extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of 18th-century English literature and theatre; readers of annotated periodicals
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative norms and standards for theatrical performance, acting, portraiture, and periodical writing as expressed in/annotated from early-18th-century Tatler items and commentary. Covers what makes good acting, what a play should do morally and intellectually, and related standards for painters and writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful characterisation / entering into the nature of the part
rubrics_metrics.description: "made a very pretty figure, and exactly entered into the nature of the part."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts are praised when the performer fully embodies the role's nature; example: Mrs. Bignell 'exactly entered into the nature of the part' of the Country Wife, producing applause. Implies accuracy of feel, behaviour, and appropriateness to the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility and vivacity in acting
rubrics_metrics.description: "variety of humour, attended with an equal vivacity, which made her excellent in characters extremely different... She was all art, but dressed so nice, it looked like nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors should display range across very different characters and sustain lively energy; versatility (comic and tragic range, low and high characters) and an animated presence are highlighted as marks of excellence (Cibber on Mrs. Mountford/Verbruggen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate physical grace for role (e.g., 'grace in her rusticity')
rubrics_metrics.description: "she made a very pretty figure... had a certain grace in her rusticity... which gave us hopes of seeing her a very skilful player."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical carriage, deportment and role-appropriate mannerisms (even in 'rustic' parts) contribute to skillful acting; small natural gestures and fitting physical style are praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-stage discretion and private character
rubrics_metrics.description: "she maintained by not being unguarded in her private character. This discretion contributed not a little to make her the darling of the theatre."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A performer’s private conduct and discretion affect public reputation and audience favour; being 'unguarded' off-stage is an anti-pattern that can diminish esteem regardless of stage talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range across tragic and comic roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The same actress succeeding 'in two very different characters' (e.g., Statira and Millamant) and 'acquitted herself with uncommon applause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to excel in both tragic and comic registers demonstrates notable range; specific role-pairs (tragic heroine vs. witty coquette) are given as illustrative tests of range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage presence beyond mere beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: "she had no greater claim to beauty... But her youth and lively aspect threw out such a glow of health and cheerfulness, that, on the stage, few spectators... could behold her without desire."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical beauty alone is not determinative; vivacity, health, cheerfulness and presence create stage allure. Emphasises that performance charisma often outweighs static attractiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre as moral/improving influence
rubrics_metrics.description: "a good play acted before a well-bred audience, must raise very proper incitements to good behaviour, and be the most quick and most prevailing method of giving young people a turn of sense and breeding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plays should promote good behaviour and social breeding when properly presented; the moral effect of dramatic representation on youth and manners is an explicit standard for theatre's social value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic representation of contemporary manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer defends characters (e.g., Horner) as 'a good representation of the age in which that comedy was written' and argues a poet should reflect the manners of his time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets/playwrights are judged by fidelity to contemporary manners; portraying 'a virtuous fine gentleman' when it contradicts the age's reality is seen as ignorance rather than virtue—plausibility and sociological truth are criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calling out indecorums and public improprieties
rubrics_metrics.description: "I shall take upon me only indecorums, improprieties, and negligences... if a fine lady thinks fit to giggle at church, or a great beau come in drunk to a play, either shall be sure to hear of it in my ensuing paper:"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical critics should police public manners by reporting and admonishing breaches of decorum in assemblies (theatre, church, etc.). Naming and shaming social improprieties is an editorial duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality over mechanical, formulaic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: "the art is become merely mechanic, and men may make themselves great that way, by as certain and infallible rules... a man may make a receipt for a poem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece criticises formulaic or 'receipt'-style composition; originality and genuine invention are implied as preferred qualities, while mechanical rule-following is derided as an inferior method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture/composition that conveys distinct types of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Clarissa is soft... Chloe piercing... Clarissa... harmony of feature, complexion, and shape; Chloe... the whole woman irresistible... Chloe drawn with a liveliness... dress of a straw hat and riband... to represent that sort of beauty which enters the heart with a certain familiarity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painters should use pose, dress, expression and composition to evoke differing kinds of beauty and their psychological effects on viewers; technical choices (pose, attire, expression) should match the intended type (artless harmony vs. piercing liveliness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the understanding — theatrical works should not be merely sensory
rubrics_metrics.description: "the stage being an entertainment of the reason and all our faculties, this way of being pleased... being given up to the shallow satisfaction of the eyes and ears only, seems to arise rather from the degeneracy of our understanding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama (and opera) should stimulate intellect and moral faculties, not merely provide sensory spectacle; productions that focus only on visual/auditory display are criticized as shallow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence of time, place and language in performance
rubrics_metrics.description: "a great critic fell into fits in the gallery, at feeling, not only time and place, but languages and nations confused in the most incorrigible manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing eras, locales, languages or national styles incoherently in a single performance is judged a serious flaw; works should maintain internal coherence of setting and language to preserve intelligibility and critical respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offending powerful persons in news writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "I avoid speaking of things which may offend great persons... I must not prostitute the liberal sciences so far, as not to utter the truth in cases which do not immediately concern the good of my native country."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical authors are advised to practice prudent self-censorship: avoid needless offence to powerful figures while remaining truthful on matters of public interest. Balances truth-telling with caution toward patrons/power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of credible correspondents/sources in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: "my correspondent, by the way of Brussels, informs me, upon his honour, that the gentleman who writes the Gazette of Paris... has told him..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should be grounded in correspondent testimony and verifiable accounts; the writer emphasizes sourcing ('upon his honour') as a way to contradict exaggerated claims in other news-writers and to lend credibility to assertions.
